When a token is dropped at a saturated expert, the residual bypass returns the token's input embedding unchanged as the "output" of that expert layer, meaning the loss gradient backpropagates through the router as if the expert computation did occur but produced an identity transformation — the router receives no explicit signal that the token was dropped. The router's softmax weight for the selected expert still gets a gradient update, but because the downstream loss is computed on the bypassed (unprocessed) token representation, the gradient direction depends entirely on whether that unprocessed representation accidentally reduces the loss — if it does, the router is rewarded for routing to the saturated expert, reinforcing the already-overloaded assignment. This mechanism was identified concretely in the Switch Transformer paper (Fedus et al., 2022): their capacity factor ablations showed that reducing C below 1.0 (forcing aggressive dropping) didn't degrade routing diversity — it concentrated it, suggesting dropped tokens were not discouraging their assigned expert. The auxiliary load-balancing loss (weighted by coefficient α, typically 0.01 in Switch-T and 0.001 in ST-MoE) operates on the mean routing probability across the batch and is too weak and too smooth to counteract the per-token gradient signal reinforcing popular experts, especially when α is kept small to avoid overwhelming the task loss. Lepikhin et al.'s GShard (2021) partially addressed this with expert-level capacity enforcement on the second expert in top-2 routing, but this only relocates the gradient distortion — overflow tokens sent to their second-choice expert still generate gradients that reflect unprocessed representations, now corrupting the second-choice expert's gradient signal as well. The compounding effect across layers is that each transformer block's router independently learns to over-assign the same experts because the per-layer auxiliary loss has no cross-layer coordination term, so imbalance discovered at layer k is invisible to the router at layer k+1 when constructing its assignments. In distributed training with expert parallelism across devices, this means specific device ranks become gradient sinks — absorbing disproportionate update signal — while others receive near-zero task-loss gradients, creating optimizer state divergence across ranks that Adam's moment estimates cannot compensate for without explicit rank-level loss rescaling.

Expert-choice routing guarantees load balance by having each expert select exactly its quota of tokens from the full sequence, but this introduces a critical failure mode: token dropping is no longer uniform — instead, the tokens not selected by any expert are systematically the ones that are semantically distant from every expert's current specialization, meaning the model learns to silently ignore tokens that don't fit its learned partition of input space, with no residual bypass signal and no gradient accountability. Zhou et al. (2022), who introduced expert-choice routing, acknowledged that in their Wikipedia and C4 experiments some tokens were selected by zero experts in early training, creating "orphan tokens" whose representations stall at their residual stream value — but they underreported how this concentrates during fine-tuning on narrow domains where token distributions shift away from pretraining geometry. The causal inference incompatibility is the more fundamental problem: expert-choice requires each expert to score all tokens in the sequence before selecting its top-K, which means position t's routing decision depends on positions t+1 through T — a future-token dependency that is structurally incompatible with autoregressive decoding where future tokens don't exist yet. Systems that train with expert-choice and deploy autoregressively (a gap that exists in several research prototypes) must switch to token-choice routing at inference, creating a train-inference routing distribution mismatch that is qualitatively different from standard train-inference discrepancies: the identity of which expert processes which token changes, not just the probabilities, so expert weight matrices encounter activation distributions they were never trained on. This mismatch is particularly damaging because expert specialization during training under expert-choice produces weight matrices tuned to a specific subset of the token distribution; when token-choice routing at inference sends a different subset to each expert, the expert receives out-of-distribution activations in exactly the layers where it has learned the sharpest functional specialization. Mixtral (Jiang et al., 2024) avoided this entire problem class by committing to token-choice top-2 routing throughout training and inference, accepting the load imbalance risk in exchange for causal consistency — a design decision that reflects the field's current pragmatic consensus that train-inference routing parity is non-negotiable for production deployment. The underappreciated compounding effect is that orphan token rates and routing distribution mismatch both worsen with sequence length: longer sequences increase the probability that rare token types appear, and rare tokens are precisely those most likely to be unselected under expert-choice and most likely to be misrouted under the token-choice fallback at inference.

When an expert receives out-of-distribution tokens, its internal LayerNorm — which has learned gain (γ) and bias (β) parameters calibrated to the mean and variance of its specialized activation subspace — applies a normalization that is statistically incorrect for the OOD input: the running statistics don't match the incoming distribution, so the normalized pre-activation sits in a region of the FFN's nonlinearity (typically SwiGLU or GELU) that was never densely trained, producing activation magnitudes that can be either saturated or near-zero depending on which tail of the OOD distribution the token lands on. The FFN gate projection in SwiGLU (used in Mixtral, LLaMA-MoE, and DeepSeek-MoE) is particularly vulnerable because the gating term σ(Wx) · (Vx) creates a multiplicative interaction: if σ(Wx) saturates near 1.0 for OOD inputs due to miscalibrated LayerNorm, the output magnitude scales with ||Vx|| unchecked, and for tokens whose projections align with high-norm directions of V — directions the expert never learned to suppress — this produces activation spikes that can exceed bf16 representable range (~65504), causing overflow to inf or NaN that propagates forward through the residual stream. This is not merely theoretical: Zoph et al. (2022) reported that ST-MoE training required router z-loss (an auxiliary term penalizing large router logit magnitudes) specifically because without it, experts receiving unexpected token distributions during early training produced logit explosions that destabilized the entire model, suggesting the FFN instability feeds back into the router's input representation. The propagation across layers is structurally guaranteed by the residual stream: an activation spike at expert layer k adds a large-magnitude vector to the residual, which becomes the input to layer k+1's attention and router, where the anomalous magnitude distorts attention logit scaling (since attention scores scale as QK^T/√d, a high-norm residual inflates all query-key dot products) and pushes the next layer's router into a logit regime it wasn't trained on, cascading the instability. DeepSeek-MoE (Dai et al., 2024) introduced a shared expert mechanism — keeping 1-2 experts always active for every token regardless of routing — partly as an implicit stabilizer, ensuring that every token has at least one expert processing it with in-distribution statistics, which acts as a soft floor on representational quality even when specialized experts produce pathological outputs. What experts miss in standard monitoring is that bf16 overflow events are silent in most distributed training frameworks: PyTorch's default behavior replaces inf/NaN with zero in gradient accumulation under some configurations, meaning an expert can be producing pathological forward outputs while its gradient signal simply vanishes — the training loss appears stable while the expert's weights drift toward a degenerate fixed point with no observable diagnostic signal. The interaction between LayerNorm parameter drift and FFN instability is self-reinforcing over training steps: once an expert's γ/β parameters are updated on OOD inputs, they move further from the values appropriate for in-distribution tokens, meaning the expert becomes progressively worse at processing both distributions simultaneously — a form of representational interference that is distinct from catastrophic forgetting but produces similar functional degradation.

The z-loss (L_z = (1/B)Σ(log Σ_e exp(x_e))², with coefficient α_z ≈ 0.001 in ST-MoE) penalizes the log-sum-exp of router logits, which gradients push toward minimization by shrinking all logits uniformly toward zero — while the auxiliary load-balancing loss penalizes deviation from uniform routing probability, which gradients satisfy by making all logits equal rather than necessarily small. These two objectives are compatible in their preferred solution — a router that outputs identical small logits for all experts — but this joint minimum is precisely the degenerate configuration where the softmax distribution is maximally uniform (equal probability 1/E per expert) and the logit magnitudes are minimized, satisfying both losses while rendering the router informationally inert: every token is routed with equal probability to every expert, destroying specialization entirely. The saddle point character of this configuration is subtle: it is a minimum of the combined auxiliary objective but a saddle point of the full loss landscape including task loss, because the task loss gradient at this point points strongly toward logit separation — however, if α_z and α_lb are both nonzero and the task loss has locally small gradients (late in training or on easy batches), the auxiliary terms can dominate and trap the router near this degenerate minimum for extended training periods. The interaction becomes particularly pathological because the z-loss gradient is proportional to the logit magnitude itself (∂L_z/∂x_e ∝ log Σ exp(x_e) · exp(x_e)/Σ exp(x_e)), meaning as logits shrink toward zero, the z-loss gradient also shrinks — so near the degenerate minimum, the z-loss provides vanishingly small corrective force while the load-balancing loss continues to push toward uniformity, creating an asymmetric gradient field that makes escape from the degenerate region progressively harder as training proceeds. In distributed training, this degenerate configuration has an additional stability property that makes it a genuine attractor: when all experts receive equal token fractions, all-to-all communication volume is perfectly balanced across ranks, eliminating the throughput variance that would otherwise create asynchronous gradient updates — so the distributed training system actually runs faster near the degenerate router configuration, and wall-clock-based early stopping criteria may incorrectly identify this as a training success. The principled resolution would require a loss term that penalizes mutual information collapse between token identity and expert assignment — something like a router entropy regularizer that rewards high routing certainty per token even while maintaining aggregate balance — but no production MoE system currently implements this, leaving practitioners reliant on ad-hoc α schedules and periodic manual inspection of expert utilization histograms.
